title: Question 7

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: The switch $S$ is now closed. As a result, the oscillations of the magnet are lightly damped.
parts.text: State what is meant by damping.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the total mechanical energy of the magnet-spring system - kinetic plus potential - as it keeps oscillating. Does it stay constant if there is any opposition to motion?
Hint 2: Focus on what does work against the motion to remove that energy. What general name do we give to forces like friction, air resistance or electromagnetic braking forces?
parts.proper_answer: Damping is the loss of energy from an oscillating system due to work done against resistive forces.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What an ideal oscillation would do**
Imagine the magnet moving up and down with no opposition at all. It would keep swapping kinetic energy for potential energy forever with no loss. In real systems this never happens.

Step 2: **Where the energy goes**
Damping means some mechanical energy is continuously taken out of the oscillation. That energy is transferred to the surroundings, often as thermal energy, because a resistive force acts opposite to velocity and does negative work: $$W = F \times d$$ against the motion.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Describe what is observed to indicate that the damping is light.

markscheme_points.text:
amplitude (of oscillations) decreases gradually
or
oscillations continue (for several periods)

hints: Hint 1: Picture the displacement-time trace. If only a tiny fraction of energy is lost per swing, how many swings will you still see and how quickly will the peaks shrink?
parts.proper_answer: The amplitude decreases gradually and the magnet continues to oscillate for many periods.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reading light damping from motion**
Light means weak energy loss per cycle. So the height of each swing, the amplitude, gets only a little bit smaller each time. You still see many clear oscillations before it stops.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: By reference to electromagnetic induction and to conservation of energy, explain why the oscillations are damped.

markscheme_points.text:
cutting of (magnetic) flux causes induced e.m.f. (in coil)
or
induced e.m.f. causes current (in resistor / circuit)

current causes dissipation of thermal energy in resistor
or
current in resistor causes dissipation of thermal energy
thermal energy comes from energy of oscillations

hints: Hint 1: Start with the magnet moving in and out of the coil. What is changing for the coil, and what does Faraday's law say this produces when the switch is closed?
Hint 2: Once there is a current in the complete circuit, think about what happens in the resistor. What form of energy appears there?
Hint 3: Link the two energy stores together. If thermal energy is appearing in the resistor but no battery is present, where must that energy have come from to satisfy conservation of energy?
parts.proper_answer: Movement of the magnet causes change of magnetic flux linkage in the coil, inducing an e.m.f. and hence a current in the closed circuit. This current dissipates thermal energy in the resistor by Joule heating. By conservation of energy this thermal energy comes from the oscillation energy, so oscillations are damped.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Induction in the coil**
As the magnet oscillates, the magnetic flux through the coil keeps changing. By Faraday's law a changing flux linkage induces an e.m.f. in the coil. Because switch S is closed, this e.m.f. drives an induced current round the circuit through the resistor.

Step 2: **Heating in the resistor**
A current in a resistor always transfers electrical energy to thermal energy. The power dissipated is $$P = I^2 R$$ so thermal energy is continuously produced while the magnet moves.

Step 3: **Paying for it with oscillation energy**
Energy cannot be created. There is no cell in the circuit, so the only source for that thermal energy is the kinetic and potential energy of the oscillating magnet and spring. Removing mechanical energy each cycle is exactly damping.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The procedure in (a) is repeated after replacing the resistor with one of greater resistance.

Suggest, with a reason, the effect of this change on the oscillations.

markscheme_points.text:
(for any given e.m.f.) current is lower so thermal energy dissipated at a lower rate
or
(for any given e.m.f.) current is lower so the resistive force is lower

oscillations are less damped
or
smaller decrease in amplitude of oscillations (in each period)
or
oscillations continue for longer

hints: Hint 1: For the same speed of magnet the induced e.m.f. is the same. Use $V = IR$ thinking to compare the current with a larger $R$.
Hint 2: Connect smaller current to the rate of thermal energy production in the resistor and hence to how fast amplitude falls.
parts.proper_answer: With greater resistance the induced current is smaller for a given e.m.f., so thermal energy is dissipated at a lower rate. Less oscillation energy is removed per cycle, so damping is lighter and oscillations persist for longer.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Smaller current for the same motion**
The e.m.f. depends only on rate of change of flux, so for the same oscillation it is unchanged. But $$I = \frac{E}{R}$$ so larger $R$ gives smaller $I$. Less current also means a weaker opposing magnetic force on the magnet.

Step 2: **Less damping**
Joule heating rate $$P = I^2 R = \frac{E^2}{R}$$ falls when $R$ increases. Less mechanical energy is drained per period, so the amplitude decreases more slowly. The oscillations are less damped and last longer.
